sections.text:
1 Asclatio qui commemoratur etiam in prooemio Vetti Valentis (ὁ Τίμαιος καὶ
ὁ Ἀσκλατίων, Catal., I, p. 79, 19), unde eum ante medium saec. II vixisse apparet,
et saec. VI apud Lydum, De ostentis, 2 (Catal., I, p. 81, 12), est, ni fallimur, celeber
ille mathematicus qui mortem Domitiani et suum ipse exitum praedixisse fertur.
Ascletario vocatur in codicibus Suetoni (Domit. 15), sed nomen corruptum esse
viri docti iam dudum animadverterunt (cf. Boissevain ad Dion. Cass., LXVII, 16,
v. 12). Ἀσκληπίονα eum appellat Malalas p. 266, 14 ed. Bonn., unde Ἀσκλήπιος
dictus est in Chron. Pasch., I, 468, 13 et in excerptis Byzantinis a Maximiliano Treu
editis (Progr. gymn. Ohlau, 1880, p. 32, 11). Revera Ἀσκλατίων nomen est
Aegyptiacum, vide Berlin. Urkunden, I, 14, c. 3, v. 10 (anni 255 p. C.). Cf. Ἀσκλατᾶς
Oxyrh. Pap., II, 297, 1 et Ἀσκλᾶς passim.
2 Notissimi sunt omnes illi astronomi, quorum nomina sine discrimine ex Pto-
lemaeo transcripsit astrologus saeculi IV.
3 Antiochus Atheniensis; cf. Catal., II, p. 83 ss. et passim.
4 Vettius Valens, celeberrimus astrologus saec. II; cf. Catal., II, p. 83 ss. et
supra p. 118, n. 2.
5 Antigonus Nicaenus, qui exeunte saeculo II aut ineunte III floruit; cf. Catal.,
IV, p. 67, n. 1.
6 Quis sit hic Heraïscus, nescimus.
7 Serapio Alexandrinus, cf. supra p. 179, n. 2.
sections.en: 1 Asclatio who is mentioned also in the preface of Vettius Valens (ὁ Τίμαιος καὶ ('Timaeus and') ὁ Ἀσκλατίων ('Asclation'), Catal., I, p. 79, 19), whence it appears that he lived before the middle of the 2nd century, and in the 6th century in Lydus, De ostentis, 2 (Catal., I, p. 81, 12), is, unless we are mistaken, that famous mathematician who is said to have predicted the death of Domitian and his own end. He is called Ascletario in the codices of Suetonius (Domit. 15), but that the name is corrupt learned men have long since noticed (cf. Boissevain ad Dion. Cass., LXVII, 16, v. 12). Ἀσκληπίονα ('Asclepion') Malalas calls him p. 266, 14 ed. Bonn., whence Ἀσκλήπιος ('Asclepius') he is called in Chron. Pasch., I, 468, 13 and in the Byzantine excerpts edited by Maximilian Treu (Progr. gymn. Ohlau, 1880, p. 32, 11). In truth Ἀσκλατίων ('Asclation') is an Egyptian name, see Berlin. Urkunden, I, 14, c. 3, v. 10 (of the year 255 A.D.). Cf. Ἀσκλατᾶς ('Asclatas') Oxyrh. Pap., II, 297, 1 and Ἀσκλᾶς ('Asclas') everywhere. 2 Very well known are all those astronomers, whose names without distinction from Ptolemy the astrologer of the 4th century transcribed. 3 Antiochus of Athens; cf. Catal., II, p. 83 ss. and everywhere. 4 Vettius Valens, the most famous astrologer of the 2nd century; cf. Catal., II, p. 83 ss. and above p. 118, n. 2. 5 Antigonus of Nicaea, who flourished at the end of the 2nd century or the beginning of the 3rd; cf. Catal., IV, p. 67, n. 1. 6 Who this Heraiscus is, we do not know. 7 Serapio of Alexandria, cf. above p. 179, n. 2.

summary.headline: Fixed Stars and Their Powers
summary.text: Astrological discussion of the fixed stars’ risings, settings, phases, and powers, including their effects on weather, good fortune, oppositions, and deaths. Authorities and observers named include Meton, Apollinarius, Euctemon, Dositheus, Calippus, Philippus, Phocis, Locris, Hipparchus, Antiochus, Vettius Valens, Antigonus, Heraiscus, Serapion, and Ptolemy.
